blocks.text:
Design a calendar system, the system that lets a user book events, invite other attendees, and set up recurring meetings, while guaranteeing that a calendar never silently double-books the same time slot and that a recurring series with an individually modified occurrence still displays correctly, indefinitely. This problem is a genuine departure from most of this project's systems, its hard core is not throughput or fan-out, it is a purely algorithmic question, how do you check whether a new interval overlaps any of thousands of existing ones without scanning them all, and how do you represent a meeting that repeats every week forever without storing every single one of those occurrences as its own row.

The two techniques that make this both correct and efficient are interval overlap detection using each calendar's own sorted structure of non-overlapping events, and recurrence expansion, storing a compact rule plus a sparse list of exceptions rather than materializing every occurrence up front.

Design a calendar system, the system that lets a user book events, invite other attendees, and set up recurring meetings, while guaranteeing that a calendar never silently double-books the same time slot and that a recurring series with an individually modified occurrence still displays correctly, indefinitely. This problem is a genuine departure from most of this project's systems, its hard core is not throughput or fan-out, it is a purely algorithmic question, how do you check whether a new interval overlaps any of thousands of existing ones without scanning them all, and how do you represent a meeting that repeats every week forever without storing every single one of those occurrences as its own row.

The two techniques that make this both correct and efficient are interval overlap detection using each calendar's own sorted structure of non-overlapping events, and recurrence expansion, storing a compact rule plus a sparse list of exceptions rather than materializing every occurrence up front.

blocks.text: A user should be able to create an event with a start and end time and invite other attendees. A new booking should be rejected if it overlaps an existing event on the same calendar. A user should be able to create a recurring event, such as a weekly meeting, and later reschedule or cancel one individual occurrence without affecting the rest of the series. A user should be able to check another user's free or busy status, and find a common free slot across multiple attendees.

blocks.alt: No double booking, correct recurring events, fast conflict and free busy checks, calendar privacy, and correctness across time zones

blocks.text: No double booking means two overlapping bookings must never both succeed, even when submitted at nearly the same instant. Correct recurring events means a weekly meeting with one rescheduled occurrence has to display correctly forever, not as a rough approximation that quietly drifts wrong over time. Fast conflict and free busy checks mean checking a new event against thousands of existing ones cannot mean scanning them one at a time. Calendar privacy means a coworker checking your availability should learn that you are busy without necessarily learning what the private event actually is. And correctness across time zones means the exact same event has to show the correct local time to attendees who are physically in different time zones.

And correctness across time zones means the exact same event has to show the correct local time to attendees who are physically in different time zones.

blocks.text: This design assumes each calendar independently guarantees its own events never overlap, and treats a fixed-interval recurrence rule, plus a sparse set of per-occurrence exceptions, as sufficient to represent recurring events without needing a fuller natural-language rule engine. Recurring events are expanded lazily, computed for whatever date range is actually being viewed or queried, rather than materialized in full up front, since a series with no end date could otherwise represent an unbounded number of rows. Calendar privacy is assumed to support at least a busy-only visibility level for non-invited viewers, covered in section 21.

blocks.text: A calendar platform at real scale might serve hundreds of millions of individual calendars, each typically holding a few thousand events including recurring series. A single recurring series can represent many thousands of individual occurrences over its lifetime without ever storing each one as its own row, since only the rule and its exceptions are persisted. At peak, tens of thousands of conflict checks and free-busy lookups might be issued per second across the platform, each expected to complete quickly regardless of how many existing events a given calendar holds.

A separate free-busy service reuses the same underlying event data to find common availability across multiple attendees at once.

class Event:
    # One concrete, non-recurring event on a calendar.
    def __init__(self, start, end):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end


class Calendar:
    # A single calendar's non-overlapping events, sorted by start time,
    # supporting an efficient conflict check against only the immediately
    # adjacent neighbors, since this calendar's own events never already overlap.
    def __init__(self):
        self.events_by_start = {}  # start time -> Event
        self.sorted_starts = []  # kept sorted, used for neighbor lookups

    def _floor_start(self, start):
        # The largest existing start time that is <= the given start.
        candidates = [s for s in self.sorted_starts if s <= start]
        return max(candidates) if candidates else None

    def _ceiling_start(self, start):
        # The smallest existing start time that is >= the given start.
        candidates = [s for s in self.sorted_starts if s >= start]
        return min(candidates) if candidates else None

    def has_conflict(self, start, end):
        before_start = self._floor_start(start)
        if before_start is not None and self.events_by_start[before_start].end > start:
            return True  # the preceding event ends after this new event starts: overlap
        after_start = self._ceiling_start(start)
        if after_start is not None and after_start < end:
            return True  # the following event starts before this new event ends: overlap
        return False

    def add_event(self, start, end):
        if self.has_conflict(start, end):
            return False
        self.events_by_start[start] = Event(start, end)
        self.sorted_starts.append(start)
        self.sorted_starts.sort()
        return True

    def all_events_sorted(self):
        return [f"{self.events_by_start[s].start}-{self.events_by_start[s].end}" for s in self.sorted_starts]


class RecurrenceRule:
    # A compact, fixed-interval recurrence rule: a start day, an interval in
    # days between occurrences, and a total occurrence count.
    def __init__(self, start_day, interval_days, occurrence_count):
        self.start_day = start_day
        self.interval_days = interval_days
        self.occurrence_count = occurrence_count


class RecurrenceExpander:
    # Expands a recurrence rule into concrete occurrence days, applying any
    # per-occurrence overrides (moved dates) or cancellations on top of the base schedule.
    def expand(self, rule, overrides, cancelled):
        result = []
        for i in range(rule.occurrence_count):
            if i in cancelled:
                continue  # this occurrence is cancelled entirely; skip it
            day = overrides.get(i, rule.start_day + i * rule.interval_days)
            result.append(day)
        return result


def main():
    calendar = Calendar()

    # Two existing events: 9:00-10:00 (540-600) and 10:30-11:30 (630-690), minutes since midnight.
    print("Add 540-600:", calendar.add_event(540, 600))
    print("Add 630-690:", calendar.add_event(630, 690))

    # A conflicting booking: 9:30-10:15 (570-615) overlaps the first event.
    print("Add 570-615 (should conflict):", calendar.add_event(570, 615))

    # A booking that fits exactly in the gap: 10:00-10:30 (600-630).
    print("Add 600-630 (should succeed):", calendar.add_event(600, 630))

    print("Final calendar events, in order:", calendar.all_events_sorted())

    # Recurrence: a weekly series starting day 0, every 7 days, 4 occurrences.
    rule = RecurrenceRule(0, 7, 4)
    expander = RecurrenceExpander()

    overrides = {2: 16}  # the 3rd occurrence (index 2, originally day 14) is moved to day 16
    cancelled = {1}  # the 2nd occurrence (index 1, day 7) is cancelled

    occurrences = expander.expand(rule, overrides, cancelled)
    print("Expanded occurrences (base 0,7,14,21 with index1 cancelled, index2 moved to 16):", occurrences)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: ["Architecture: per-calendar interval-overlap conflict checking, lazy recurrence expansion from rules and exceptions, and a free-busy service merging attendees' busy intervals.","Capacity: hundreds of millions of calendars, a few thousand events per typical calendar, and tens of thousands of conflict and free-busy checks per second at peak.","The core techniques: efficient interval overlap detection against sorted, non-overlapping events, and recurrence expansion with sparse exceptions, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.","Database: a calendar-partitioned event store alongside a comparatively small, sparse recurrence rule and exception store.","End-to-end workflows: a normal booking flow and a recurrence expansion query, both traced as sequence diagrams.","Consistency: a strongly consistent, atomic conflict-check-and-insert per calendar, paired with an eventually consistent shared free-busy view.","Trade-offs: lazy rule-plus-exception expansion versus materializing every occurrence upfront versus no recurrence support at all, compared directly on storage cost and where each breaks down."]
items: Architecture: per-calendar interval-overlap conflict checking, lazy recurrence expansion from rules and exceptions, and a free-busy service merging attendees' busy intervals.
Capacity: hundreds of millions of calendars, a few thousand events per typical calendar, and tens of thousands of conflict and free-busy checks per second at peak.

The core techniques: efficient interval overlap detection against sorted, non-overlapping events, and recurrence expansion with sparse exceptions, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a calendar-partitioned event store alongside a comparatively small, sparse recurrence rule and exception store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal booking flow and a recurrence expansion query, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent, atomic conflict-check-and-insert per calendar, paired with an eventually consistent shared free-busy view.
Trade-offs: lazy rule-plus-exception expansion versus materializing every occurrence upfront versus no recurrence support at all, compared directly on storage cost and where each breaks down.
